code.text: On the table: a board of nine cells in three rows of three, numbered 0 to 8 row by row. The win check tests eight index triples, rows 0-1-2, 3-4-5 and 6-7-8, columns 0-3-6, 1-4-7 and 2-5-8, diagonals 0-4-8 and 2-4-6, for three equal non-empty marks. A draw is a full board with no triple; a line completed on the ninth move is a win, which a full-board check alone would miss. The reference source restarts by clearing every cell, enabling every cell and hiding the message, and its status line names the winner after a win. Its three local files are the three pieces a one-file build folds into one. A tutorial build lays the board out as a three-column CSS grid of numbered cells, and its pointer targets run at 24 CSS pixels or more. The status line can sit in a live region so a screen reader hears each change. Ways in: from the nine-cell round with one status line; from the finish, where the status names the result and the cells stop taking marks; from the solved game, where a level round is a real ending; from the three-file layout, folded into one file. Dials: basic as the minimal complete round, as a complete but plain page with named players, a marked winning line and keyboard use with a focus ring, or as a bare logic core with no page. Code size from a few lines that still play to a file of named functions a reader follows aloud. Board state as a flat list of nine, a two-dimensional grid, or one bit mask per player. Result display as status text alone, the three winning cells marked, or both. Marks as letters X and O, an icon cross and open circle, or a hand-drawn stroke, in one colour or two far-apart hues, with the shapes doing the telling. Focus after restart as the first empty cell, the restart button, or the status line. Worn paths: the usual move is a settings screen, a theme switcher, sound effects or a score that carries across rounds; the round itself can stay plain, with each of those as a listed reading. The usual move for a result is a colour change alone; a sentence in the status line with the winning cells marked a second way is another reading. The usual move for a taken cell is a silent overwrite; a click that changes nothing, with the turn and the status left as they were, or a short refusal line, is another reading. Open: whether there is a computer opponent (the readings include two players on one device and a computer player), whether a tally carries across restarts, and the look, where plain system fonts and neutral colours are one reading among several.
code.constraints: One HTML file with the CSS and JavaScript inline and no external URL, font or CDN, as the consumer names it. One option: native buttons for the cells, so a click, a tap, Tab focus and Enter or Space all place a mark.

params.file: one HTML file, CSS and script inline

code.notes: Choices, not requirements: the opponent, the marks, the result display, the restart behaviour and the board state are options in game_rules and play_feedback. The payload lists them as readings only.

check_output.text: Play one round through each state, from the first move to restart, and answer each review prompt from the screen or the page state: does a mark open the round, and does the status name whose move it is after each move; does a line of three in any of the eight triples name its winner, and does a full board with no line name a draw; does a click on a taken cell leave the mark and the turn as they were, and does a click after the end change nothing; does restart clear the cells and the result; does a marked winning line sit on the cells that won, with the status still naming the winner; does the file load nothing from outside, and does the console stay free of errors; can a keyboard user place a mark, and does a screen reader hear each change in the status line. Each question is a question worth asking of an output, not a verdict: a no on one points at the rule it names, and the consumer may explain a deliberate deviation.

ak-lx-basic.excluded_sense: a settings panel, theme picker, score tally or sound effects added on top of the round itself; computer opponents and win tallies stay as options (opt-opponent, opt-restart)
ak-lx-basic.instead: a bare complete round; a plain complete round with named players and a winning-line highlight; a small polished page

ak-lx-game.excluded_sense: a game engine, game library, framework or app store listing
ak-lx-game.instead: a playable page: two players, one board, one round at a time

ak-lx-tic-tac-toe.excluded_sense: the 4x4 or 5x5 variants, and gomoku or five in a row on a large board
ak-lx-tic-tac-toe.instead: the 3x3 game of three in a row, noughts and crosses

ak-restart-broken.instead: A restart button that empties all nine cells, makes each one clickable again, and sets X to move first.
ak-restart-broken.text: Forbidden shortcut: a board that cannot be restarted in the page forces a reload and breaks the play-again job.

ak-debug-logging.instead: No logging in the shipped file; the win and draw checks stay silent and only the status line reports results.
ak-debug-logging.text: The reference source keeps console.log calls in its win check. Leftover debug output is noise in a finished file.

ak-noise-stunning.instead: A board that reads at a glance: crisp grid, legible X and O, a result in words.

ak-noise-robust.instead: Exact rules under every move order: checked wins, refused illegal moves, a restart that resets everything.

ak-noise-masterpiece.instead: A finished small page: a clear status line, an obvious next move, one restart.

ak-settings-panel.instead: Open straight into a playable round: two players on one board, X first, nothing to set up.
ak-settings-panel.text: One reading of basic leaves a settings screen out, since it adds steps before the first move. A fuller page can add one.

ak-theme-switcher.instead: One plain colour scheme with high-contrast marks and text that follows the system light or dark setting.
ak-theme-switcher.text: One reading of basic leaves themes out; the board needs only clear marks and readable text. A fuller page can add a theme.

ak-sound-effects.instead: Silent play: every result is written in words on the page, so sound is never needed to know what happened.
ak-sound-effects.text: One reading of basic leaves sound out; the result stays readable in words either way. A fuller page can add sound.

ak-carried-score.instead: Each round stands alone: restart clears the board and the status and starts a fresh round with X first.
ak-carried-score.text: Unless the user asks for a tally, one round stands alone; the tally option is listed under options.

ak-external-library.instead: One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and script, system fonts, and marks drawn as text or CSS shapes.
ak-external-library.text: A one-file page runs offline. A library or CDN adds external requests and a dependency the basic round does not need.

variants: board still active after a win
ak-move-after-end.instead: Once the result shows, empty cells ignore clicks and the final board stays visible until the restart.
ak-move-after-end.text: A mark placed after a win or draw changes a finished result. The board can lock when the round ends.

ak-animation-delay.instead: A mark appears the moment it is placed and the status changes at once.
ak-animation-delay.text: An animation that holds input back makes the game feel slow. Feedback should be immediate.

ak-no-result.instead: Every finished round ends in words in the status line, such as 'X wins' or 'Draw'.
ak-no-result.text: A round that ends silently leaves the player guessing. The end state needs its own visible words.

ak-colour-only-result.instead: Words in the status line, such as 'O wins' or 'Draw'; colour may add to them, never replace them.
ak-colour-only-result.text: Forbidden shortcut: a result shown only by a colour change is invisible to colour-blind players and to screen readers.

variants: clicking a filled cell replaces the mark
turn passes on a filled cell
ak-overwrite-filled-cell.instead: A click on a filled cell does nothing; the turn and the status line stay as they were.
ak-overwrite-filled-cell.text: Accepting a move on a taken cell breaks the rules of the game and corrupts the board state.

ak-partial-win-check.instead: All eight lines are tested after every move, so a line of three always ends the round.
ak-partial-win-check.text: A check that skips a line lets a real win go unnoticed. Testing the eight fixed triples covers every case.

variants: div cells with click handlers only
ak-inaccessible-cells.instead: Nine real buttons named by row and column, played with Tab and Enter or Space, with a polite live status.
ak-inaccessible-cells.text: Cells that are only clickable boxes cannot be placed by keyboard or heard by a screen reader.

ak-board-overflow.term: board wider than the phone screen
variants: board cut off at the bottom
ak-board-overflow.instead: A square board scaled to the smaller screen side, each cell at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels.
ak-board-overflow.text: A fixed-size board can run off a phone. Targets smaller than 24 CSS pixels miss WCAG 2.5.8.

ak-bigger-board.instead: Exactly 3x3, three in a row to win, nine cells, X first: the noughts and crosses rules.
ak-bigger-board.text: The prompt names tic tac toe, a 3x3 game of three in a row. Larger boards and other win lengths are different games.

k-first-mark.text: Which mark opens the round, and does the first status line name that player for the first move? The usual convention is X, and the choice stays open (opt-first-mark).

test.spec: Load the page; the first status line names one player for the first move, and the first mark placed is that player's mark.

k-status-alternate.text: After each legal move, does the status line name the player whose move it is, or the result?

test.spec: Place five moves in turn and read the status line after each one; it names the next player or the result.

k-eight-triples.text: Does a line of three end the round on each of the eight lines, three rows, three columns and two diagonals, whatever form the win check takes?

test.spec: For each of the eight lines in turn, play that line for one mark in a fresh round; each ends the round and names that mark as the winner, however the check is written.

k-draw.text: Does a full board with no line of three name a draw?

test.spec: Play X 0, O 1, X 2, O 4, X 3, O 5, X 7, O 6, X 8; the status reads a draw and names no winner.

k-ninth-move-win.text: Does a ninth move that completes a line report the win rather than a draw?

test.spec: Play X 0, O 1, X 4, O 3, X 6, O 2, X 7, O 5, X 8; the status names X as the winner, not a draw.

k-taken-cell.text: Does a click on a taken cell leave the mark and the turn as they were, with the status either unchanged or giving a short refusal?

test.spec: Click an occupied cell during play; the mark and the turn stay the same, and the status line either keeps its text or shows a short refusal such as 'That cell is taken'.

k-after-end.text: After a win or a draw, does a click on an empty cell change nothing?

test.spec: Finish a round, then click an empty cell; no mark appears and the result text stays.

k-keyboard-place.text: Can a keyboard user reach each empty cell with Tab and place a mark with Enter or Space?

test.spec: Tab through the board from the start of the page; each empty cell takes focus and Enter or Space places the mark.

k-no-external.text: Does the file load nothing from outside: no script, stylesheet, font or image address?

test.spec: no src= or href= attribute with http:// or https://, and no @import or url() pointing at http:// or https://

k-status-win.text: After a win, does the status line name the winner in words?

test.spec: After a win the status text reads with the winning mark X or O, not colour alone.

k-restart.text: Does restart clear all nine cells and the result text?

test.spec: Finish a round and press restart: nine empty cells, all enabled, and no result text.

k-live-status.text: Does the status line sit in a live region, so a screen reader hears each change?

test.spec: the status element carries role="status" or aria-live="polite"

k-colour-not-alone.text: Do X and O differ by shape or text as well as colour?

test.spec: Render the board in greyscale; X and O remain distinct.

k-cell-targets.text: Are the cells and the restart control at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels on a phone?

test.spec: At a 390 px wide viewport, the bounding box of each cell and the restart button is at least 24 px on each side.

k-basic-scope.text: Does the page stay a basic round, one board, a status line and a restart, without settings, themes, scores or sound nobody asked for?

test.spec: List the controls: a board, a status line and a restart; no settings, theme, score or sound control appears.

k-no-debug.text: Does the script leave debug output behind?

test.spec: no console.log call in the shipped script

k-winline-cue.text: When a line wins, do its three cells differ from the rest by weight or a border as well as colour, with the status line still naming the winner?

test.spec: Win on the anti-diagonal and render in greyscale; the three winning cells stand apart from the rest, and the status text names the winner.

k-runtime-errors.text: Does the page load and play through a win, a draw, a refused click and a restart with no uncaught error in the console?

test.spec: Open the console, load the page and play each state once; no uncaught exception appears, and the status keeps updating after each step.

pr-system-status.text: Nielsen's first heuristic: keep the player informed about what is happening, with timely feedback.
pr-system-status.quote: The design should always keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within a reasonable amount of time.
pr-system-status.principle: Players act on what they can see; the status line must always say whose turn it is or how the round ended.
behaviors: The status line names the current player after every move
A win or draw replaces the turn text at once
The status line is never left showing a stale turn

pr-hick-fitts.term: Hick's law and Fitts's law for cell targets
pr-hick-fitts.text: Decision time grows with the number of choices; reach time grows with distance and shrinks with target size.
pr-hick-fitts.quote: The time to acquire a target is a function of the distance to and size of the target.
pr-hick-fitts.principle: Nine equal, large cells that are only a few choices at a time are fast to read and hit.
behaviors: Nine cells, each choice visible at once, keeps the decision cheap
Cells sized as large as the board allows shorten the time to hit one
Only empty cells need a live hover or press state
signals: cells much smaller than a fingertip on phones
extra controls competing with the board

pr-target-size.text: Pointer targets must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or meet a spacing exception.
pr-target-size.quote: The size of the target for pointer inputs is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, except when
pr-target-size.principle: A board cell and the restart button should be far above the floor; the cells are the largest targets on the page.
behaviors: Each cell is at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, usually much more on a phone
Padding can enlarge a small restart button's hit area

pr-use-of-colour.text: Colour alone must not carry meaning; add shape or text to mark X and O and the winning cells.
pr-use-of-colour.quote: Use information in addition to color, such as shape or text, to convey meaning.
pr-use-of-colour.principle: X and O are letters, not just colours; a red-green difference cannot be the only sign of a win.
behaviors: X and O are written as letters, not only coloured
The winning line gets a text or outline cue as well as colour
signals: players told apart only by colour

pr-live-status.text: Changing status text is announced by screen readers only inside a live region, here role status with polite.
pr-live-status.quote: A status bar or area of the screen that provides an updated status of some kind.
pr-live-status.principle: A screen reader user hears the turn and the result without losing focus on the board.
behaviors: The status element carries role status and a redundant aria-live polite
The region exists in the markup before the first update

behaviors: Option A works in greyscale because it adds a border or weight rather than a colour
Option B reads faster at a glance and needs the text cue too, so it does not rely on colour alone
With no highlight at all, the status line carries the result alone; the scraped reference has no highlight
pf-winline.principle: A win is shown twice, in text and in place, without relying on colour alone.
signals: three cells marked the same way

pf-input.text: Each cell can be a native button, so a click, a tap, Tab focus and Enter or Space all place a mark.
behaviors: A native button gets focus and key handling without extra script
Tab order follows the reading order of the grid, left to right and top to bottom
A disabled cell takes no focus, so focus moves past filled cells
signals: div cells with click handlers and no tabindex
no focus ring on the board
Enter does nothing on a focused cell

pf-labels.text: Each cell has an accessible name that gives its row, column and content, so a screen reader reads the board as a grid.
properties: grid or group role on the board
behaviors: A filled cell's name changes to its mark when it is played
Each empty cell's name stays the same across moves, so the reader hears the same label for the same square
signals: no row or column in the label

pf-finish.term: finish: hover, focus and the end state
pf-finish.text: A small game feels finished when empty cells show a hover state, focus is visible, and the end state is unmistakable.
behaviors: Hover shows on empty cells, so a filled cell does not look clickable
A finished board disables its cells and puts the result in the status line
The focus ring is drawn on the cell edge in a colour with enough contrast to see on the page background
pf-finish.principle: Each state looks different from the next, so the player can tell at a glance whether a move is still possible.
signals: cells still clickable after a win

pf-check-winline.text: When a build shows a winning-line cue, the three winning cells differ from the rest in a way that is not colour alone, and the status line still names the winner. Whether to show the cue is in pf-winline.
properties: non-colour cue: border, weight or a drawn line
behaviors: A cue on the three winning cells shows which line won without reading the status
A win on a row, a column and each diagonal shows the cue on that line
pf-check-winline.principle: The cue sits on the cells that won, so the player can see the line, and the status text repeats the result for a reader who cannot see the board.
signals: three cells marked the same way
a win on the anti-diagonal with no cue on it
cue visible only as a colour change when rendered in greyscale
pf-check-winline.how_to_check: Play a win along a row, a column and each diagonal in turn, and look for the cue on exactly the three winning cells. Render the page in greyscale and check the cue is still there. A build with no cue is a plain choice from pf-winline, not a fault.

heading_path: Tic Tac Toe Game using HTML CSS & JavaScript
Tic Tac Toe Game in JavaScript [Source Codes]

cng-status.text: The status line shows X's Turn or O's Turn; a win shows a winner line and a replay button, a draw shows “Match has been drawn!”.
behaviors: Turn text switches on each move through a sliding highlight
A win or draw hides the board and shows the result box after a short delay (about 700 ms in the script)
A win or a draw replaces the turn text at once and does not wait for a restart
The tutorial shows no turn text during play; only results appear in its status area

pf-phone.text: The board scales to the screen so each cell stays a large target and the page does not scroll sideways.
properties: cells at least 24 by 24 CSS px
restart button padded to a larger hit area
behaviors: The WCAG 2.5.8 floor is 24 by 24 CSS px; cells well above it are easier to hit with a thumb
Padding enlarges a small restart button's hit area without changing its look
Three cells plus gaps fit a 390 px wide phone with room for a gutter at the sizes below

meaning.44: enhanced target size (WCAG 2.5.5), the most generous floor
meaning.64: comfortable thumb reach on a 390 px wide phone
meaning.90: the scraped desktop cell size, which still fits a 390 px phone in portrait

heading_path: Tic Tac Toe Game using HTML CSS & JavaScript

cng-layout.text: Nine square cells in three rows of three, centred on the page; one tutorial uses 90 px cells, another 50 px, each with a small gap.
properties: CSS grid, three columns of auto width
behaviors: Cells are fixed-size, so the board keeps its shape on a narrow screen only if the page scales it
Inner borders come from nth-child selectors, so the outer edge has no border
signals: fixed 50px cells with no width breakpoint in the tutorial CSS (inferred from the chunks: no media query appears)

pf-board.text: Nine equal square cells in three rows of three, centred on the page, with a small gap between cells.
behaviors: A fixed cell size keeps the board square on desktop but overflows a narrow phone unless the board scales
Sizing the board to the smaller of viewport width or height keeps the grid square on both desktop and phone
Filled cells lose their hover state, so the board reads as a set of choices and a set of marks
pf-board.principle: Nine large equal cells are quick to read and hit, and the board is the largest thing on screen.

moodboard._about: Images collected for the board (23 found online, 0 user-supplied). The described ones show the board, its target sizes, its status announcements and its palette; the rest are listed as left out. Seed material to look at, not requirements.

mb-commons-board.term: hand-drawn red X and O board
mb-commons-board.text: A hand-drawn tic-tac-toe board in saturated red marker: a crowded, messy grid of X and O marks that reads as a sketch of the game.

mb-github-sage-window.term: sage backdrop with white app window
mb-github-sage-window.text: A repository preview card: a single white app window floating on a muted sage backdrop, with plain horizontal rules and no decoration.

mb-codingnepal-blue-tiles.term: sky-blue field with white tile grid
mb-codingnepal-blue-tiles.text: A tutorial header in sky blue: a three-by-three grid of white tiles, each holding a bold white X or O, set in a flat solid field.

mb-nrich-lime-numbered.term: lime field with numbered edge cells
mb-nrich-lime-numbered.text: A puzzle-page board on lime yellow, with loose green and magenta grid lines and numerals placed on the outer cells.

mb-webtips-numbered.text: A plain board with thick black lines and bold numerals 0 to 8 in the cells, so a cell can be named by its number.

mb-webtips-hover-cursor.term: empty board with hand cursor on a cell
mb-webtips-hover-cursor.text: An empty three-by-three board in white and black, with a pointing-hand cursor over one empty cell to show it is clickable.

mb-shared-board-shape.term: square board with plain thick grid
mb-shared-board-shape.text: Most board images are a square of equal cells with plain thick lines on white, or a saturated field with white tiles; the grid carries the shape.
behaviors: A cell with a pointer over it shows a hand cursor, so the empty cell reads as a target
Numbered cells name a position without any mark

mb-palette-spread.term: sampled palettes of the collected images
behaviors: Each sampled field carries one strong colour on a plain background, so marks stand out from the board
mb-palette-spread.text: Three sampled palettes far apart: deep red on white, sky blue with white tiles, and lime yellow with green and magenta lines.

mb-wcag-target-24.text: A technical figure showing three 24 by 24 CSS pixel square targets side by side, with the dimension annotated on each edge.
behaviors: A rounded or skewed target needs more room to pass, so a square board cell is the simplest target shape

mb-voiceover-live.term: screen reader announcing a live update
mb-voiceover-live.text: A screenshot of a screen reader announcing a status change, with the spoken text echoed as a dark caption bar under the page.
behaviors: A status text that changes is announced by a screen reader only when it sits in a live region

mb-images-not-described.text: Collected, looked at, and left out (15): target-figure variants, dark and chrome variants, site logos, a text-led title card, a duplicate, off-topic images and transparent thumbnails.

game_rules._about: The rules a basic tic tac toe game keeps: turns, win lines, draw, refused moves, board state, restart, and what an output shows for each. Facets and options, not a finished game.

options._about: options, not requirements: decisions the rules leave open, each with what it includes and what it costs in code and in the word basic

opt-result-display.decision: how a result shows on the board
opt-result-display.text: Three options. The status line carries the result in every option; the choice is what else marks the board.

options.includes: a result sentence naming the winner or a draw
options.cost: cheapest; a screen reader hears it through the live status
options.fits_when: the user wants the plainest finish

options.includes: the matched triple is already known from the win check, so the three cells get a class
options.cost: a small amount of CSS and one lookup; colour works best as a second cue (pr-use-of-colour)
options.fits_when: the user wants the win to be seen on the board

options.includes: status text and the highlighted triple
options.cost: both costs together; still a small page
options.fits_when: the user wants a clear finish without relying on colour alone

opt-board-state.decision: which representation holds the nine cells
opt-board-state.text: Three forms, with their trade-offs in gr-board-state.

options.fits_when: the eight triples are used as written
the markup and the board read as rows
compact checks matter more than readability

opt-first-mark.decision: which mark makes the first move
opt-first-mark.text: X first is the usual convention, and the rules leave the choice open (gr-turns). Three options, each with its tradeoff.

options.includes: the convention most rules and the scraped reference use (tt-first)
options.fits_when: the user expects the familiar opener

options.includes: the other mark opens; the turn rule is unchanged
options.fits_when: the user wants O to open

options.option: a player chooses the first mark
options.includes: a choice before the first move, or a restart that asks who opens
options.cost: an extra control and state; the most code of the three
options.fits_when: the user wants the opener to change between rounds

signals: the status names the player for the first move
the first mark matches the choice the build made

opt-opponent.text: Four options; only the first adds nothing to the rules above.

options.includes: turns and clicks; the rules above are the whole game
options.cost: least code; the default reading of basic
options.fits_when: the user wants a plain two-player board

options.includes: a search over the game tree that picks a best move; from the start it cannot lose, since perfect play is a forced draw (tt-solved)
options.cost: a recursive search or a table; the most code
options.fits_when: the user wants an opponent no one can beat
a warm-up opponent for checking turns and the end of a round

options.includes: win, then block, then fork, in priority order (tt-priority-opponent), else a random empty cell
options.cost: a short priority list; with only win and block it can lose
options.fits_when: the user wants a game that plays back but can be beaten

opt-restart.decision: what restart keeps and what it clears, including the turn
opt-restart.text: Three options, from smallest reset to full reset. A win tally that survives restarts is its own option (pf-opt-tally); the first-mark choice is opt-first-mark.

options.includes: nine empty cells, cells enabled, result cleared; the turn is not touched (src-restart)
options.fits_when: the user wants the smallest reset

options.option: clears the board and returns the turn to the first player
options.includes: the board reset plus the first-player convention (gr-turns)
options.fits_when: every round should open the same way

options.includes: the turn goes back to the first player and the first mark is chosen again (opt-first-mark)
options.cost: an extra choice on the restart path
options.fits_when: the user wants the opener to change each round

inv-three-in-a-row.invariant: three equal marks in one row, column or diagonal end the round as a win for that mark
inv-three-in-a-row.variable: how the win is shown (status text, a highlight, or both) and where the marks are drawn
inv-three-in-a-row.scope: every output of a tic tac toe game
inv-three-in-a-row.text: Three in a row ends the round at once, whichever player made it and whichever of the eight lines it sits on.

gr-restart.text: Restart returns the board to nine empty cells, enables every cell and clears the result. The turn is a choice with two readings, both in opt-restart: back to the first player, or kept.
behaviors: Reading one, turn back to the first player: every round opens the same way
Reading two, keep the turn: the reference restart (src-restart) clears cells and message and leaves the turn alone, since the source has no turn to reset (src-missing)
Whether a win tally survives a restart is a third choice, listed under options
gr-restart.principle: A restart that leaves a locked cell or stale message behind reads as a bug; the turn can go either way if the choice is deliberate.
signals: status still shows the old result
first move after restart goes to a player the build's chosen reading does not name

gr-refused-status.text: Two readings of a refused click, both kept: the status line stays as it was, or a short line in the status line says why.

options.includes: the status line keeps its last text; the board, the mark and the turn stay as they were
options.fits_when: the user wants the quietest board

options.includes: one line in the status line, for example 'That cell is taken', 'Pick an empty square' or 'Game over: press Restart'
options.cost: a few strings and a status update per refusal
options.fits_when: the user wants the refusal explained

behaviors: A message in a live status region is read aloud, so a refusal is heard as well as seen
A silent refusal gives a sighted player no new text, only the unchanged board
gr-refused-status.principle: Whichever reading is built, the thing that has to hold is the board, the mark and the turn.
signals: status text changes to a refusal line after a rejected click
status text is identical before and after a rejected click

gr-rule-checks.text: One question per rule, asked of a built output: play it through and answer each question from the screen or the state.
questions: Which mark makes the first move, and does it match the choice the build made (opt-first-mark)?
Do the marks alternate, with no move out of turn?
Does a click on a taken cell leave the mark and the turn as they were?
After a win, does a click on an empty cell change nothing?
Does three in a row name the winner in the status?
Does a full board with no line show a draw?
After every legal move, does the status name whose move it is?
Does restart clear all nine cells and the result, and does its turn follow the restart option the build chose (opt-restart)?
Does the win check detect a win on each of the eight lines, whatever its form (gr-win-check-forms)?
Does the page play a full round with no uncaught error (gr-runtime-errors)?
signals: each question has a yes or no answer read from the screen or the state
a no on any question points at the rule it names

gr-runtime-errors.text: A built page loads and plays a full round with no uncaught error in the console. The stretch to watch covers load, a win, a draw, a refused click and a restart.
behaviors: A script error on load can leave the board unclickable with no visible message
An error thrown during a click can stop the status from updating, so the screen looks stuck on the last state
A mistyped element id is a common cause of an error on load
gr-runtime-errors.principle: A script that stops partway leaves the screen stale, which a player reads as a broken game.
signals: uncaught error in the console on load
gr-runtime-errors.how_to_check: Open the file with the console visible, then play a win, a draw, a refused click and a restart, noting any uncaught exception. A console.log line is not an error; it is covered by ak-debug-logging.

gr-draw.text: A draw is all nine cells filled with no winning triple. The check runs after every move, and a line completed on the ninth move is a win, not a draw.
properties: a tutorial counts enabled cells, zero enabled means draw
behaviors: A board-full check alone calls a win on the ninth move a draw
Running the win check before the draw check keeps the win first
A draw ends the round the same way a win does, so further moves are refused
With perfect play from both sides the game ends in a draw (tt-solved), which is why a draw is a normal ending, not a failure
gr-draw.principle: A full board with no line is a draw; checking it after the win rule keeps the win first.
signals: status says draw while a line of three is visible
no result text after the ninth mark with no line

gr-win-lines.term: eight winning lines and the win check
gr-win-lines.text: Cells numbered 0 to 8 row by row give eight index triples: three rows, three columns and two diagonals. A triple wins when its three cells hold the same non-empty mark.
properties: loop over triples, return the first non-empty equal mark
behaviors: The centre cell sits on four lines, each corner on three and each edge on two
Checking all eight triples finds a win made anywhere on the board, not only on the line of the last move
Without the non-empty test, empty cells match each other and report a winner at the start; a check on only two cells misses or invents wins
gr-win-lines.principle: A fixed list of triples turns win detection into a lookup over eight known sets instead of a search.
signals: three equal marks in one triple
a win reported on an empty board
a win recognised only when the last move sits on its line

gr-board-state.text: Three ways to hold the nine cells. Each trades readability against the work that a win check and a redraw need.

representations.form: flat list of nine, indexed 0 to 8
representations.tradeoff: the eight triples index it directly; a row or column is index arithmetic

representations.form: two-dimensional grid, three rows of three
representations.tradeoff: reads like the board; rows and columns are loops, and the diagonals need explicit index pairs

representations.form: one bit mask per player over nine bits
representations.tradeoff: a win is one AND test per player against eight masks; a full board is 511; compact, hard to read at a glance

behaviors: Whichever form is chosen, the status and the redraw read from the same state, so the screen does not drift from it
A win check that reads the buttons instead of the state ties the rules to the markup
gr-board-state.principle: One source of truth for the board; the display is a view of it.
signals: the win check reads the button text
two copies of the board that can disagree

gr-turns.text: Marks alternate one move each until a result or a full board. X opening is the usual convention; which mark opens is a choice with options (opt-first-mark).
properties: X moves first in the usual convention
behaviors: The turn passes only after a legal move, so a refused click leaves the turn with the same player
Who starts is a convention, not a settled rule: Wikipedia says no universally agreed rule exists (tt-first)
A page with a computer opponent can let the human open and then answer with the other mark; turns still alternate (cng-turns)
gr-turns.principle: Whose move it is gets checked first; one visible owner for the next move keeps it from being guessed.
signals: status names the player whose move it is
X count is equal to O count or one more after any move

gr-refused-moves.text: A click on an occupied cell, or on any cell after a result, changes no mark and no turn. The status line either stays as it was or says why (gr-refused-status).
behaviors: A refused click keeps the turn with the same player
Disabling the cells after a result makes the refusal visible to the eye and to assistive technology
A short message in the status line explains a refusal without pulling focus off the board
gr-refused-moves.principle: Whichever reading is built, the thing that has to hold is the board, the mark and the turn.
signals: a cell's mark changes after it was taken
the status flips to the other player after a rejected click
cells on a finished board still respond to clicks

gr-win-check-forms.text: Several correct win checks exist: literal triples, a loop over a triples list, a compressed one-expression test, or lines built from rows and columns. Verify that each of the eight lines wins; the code's form is the builder's choice.
properties: lines built from rows and columns
behaviors: A compressed test passes when it wins on all eight lines and fails when it misses one
A literal list is easier to read by eye; a compressed test is shorter and harder to check by eye
Ids read from markup are strings: a numeric triple never equals a string cell, so every check fails quietly
gr-win-check-forms.principle: The eight lines are the rule; the code that tests them is free to vary, as long as cell ids and triples share one type.
signals: a win on each of the eight lines is detected
a win on one line, such as the anti-diagonal, is missed
a win reported on an empty board

vocabulary._about: Words and associations for the game and its parts. Seed material, inferred from general knowledge unless a fetched source is named elsewhere; it widens the work and defines nothing.

registers._about: Keyword taxonomy: one facet per register, each a list of short phrases for the same things from several directions.

lx-technical.text: The words a developer uses for the parts of a small board game in code and markup.

lx-perceptual.text: How the board and marks look and feel, in plain sensory words.

lx-lineage.text: Where the game comes from and the words its history brings with it.

lx-objects.text: The nouns a player meets on screen, each a candidate label, status phrase or control name.

associations._about: Things that widen the game: other games with the same shape, the pencil-and-paper and parlour tradition, other two-player grid games. Seed material, not facts. At least a third of each list is a deep cut.

as-pencil-paper.text: Two-player games played with a pencil on squared paper, or with a board drawn in chalk or carved into wood and stone.
contribution: Dots and boxes: closing a box scores it and gives another turn, so the status line shows who moves again
Sprouts: the game ends when no legal move is left, so the last move decides the result
Battleship on squared paper: a hidden grid guessed by coordinate, with hits and misses reported back
Paper soccer: a moving piece leaves a trail that limits its next step
Nine men's morris: cut into church steps, stone and tables, with pieces sliding along the lines
Fox and geese: one side controls the fox and the geese try to trap it on a drawn cross

as-grid-games.text: Two-player games on a grid or lines, with the one rule each adds to placing marks.
contribution: Othello: a placed mark flips the opponent's marks in lines, so the board changes under the play
Go: captured groups come off the board, and the play is on the crossings of the lines
Konane: a piece jumps a neighbour and removes it, from a start where the colours alternate
Bagh-chal: one side has a few tigers hunting many goats on a 5x5 board, unequal from the start
Quoridor: walls are placed to lengthen the opponent's path, so the board becomes a maze
Checkers: diagonal moves with captures that can be forced, so a move can give up a piece on purpose
Mancala: seeds are sown around pits, a sowing board rather than a line-up grid

as-same-shape.term: other games with the same shape
as-same-shape.text: Games that place marks or move pieces on a small grid to make a line, each with the one idea it adds.
contribution: Terni lapilli: after three pieces each, moves slide to a neighbouring point
Tapatan: three pieces each on a 3x3 grid, so blocking takes most of the play
Three men's morris: play runs along drawn lines, not inside squares
Misère tic tac toe: making three in a row loses, which turns the win check upside down
Qubic: the same line idea in 4x4x4, where the first player wins with best play
Hex: connect opposite sides on hexagons; a finished board cannot be a draw
Pente: captured pairs come off, so a line of three can be broken
Connect Four: gravity; a dropped piece lands on the lowest free cell of its column
Gomoku: five in a row on a large board
Ultimate tic tac toe: each cell is a smaller board, and where you play sends your opponent to a board

influences._about: Lineages and what each brings. Contributions, not styles to copy.

inf-early-machines.text: Early machines that played the game, from a computer opponent on a 1950s mainframe to a learner built from matchboxes.
contribution: a computer as the second player, the first human-against-machine round
a learner that improves from winning and losing, one game at a time
a demonstration that the game is small enough to be solved on paper

inf-tutorial.text: Small single-page builds of the game that teach the DOM and state with plain script and no framework.
contribution: an array of the eight winning index triples checked after each move
one click handler on the board, with the cell read from the element
a status element that is rewritten at each state change

quality._about: Quality readings for the prompt's word 'basic'. Each reading runs from a light hint to its full strength. None is the default; the consumer picks and mixes.

q-basic-scope.text: 'Basic' names how much of the game to build, from a bare round to a plain finished page.

readings.in_practice: Nine cells, a status line, a restart; no names, scores or sound. At full strength: nine cells and one line of text.
Player names typed first, the winning line marked, keyboard use with a focus ring. At full strength every state has its own text.
A board module with place, winner and draw functions and no page. At full strength a test plays a whole round through them.
A text-only board in a preformatted block, cells numbered 1 to 9 typed as keys, no stylesheet. At full strength one document with no CSS.

q-basic-code.text: 'Basic' for the source: how small the file is and how plainly it reads.

readings.reading: under about a hundred lines in one file
readings.in_practice: Markup, CSS and script in one file, the script a few dozen lines of plain functions. At full strength the file fits on one screen.
signals: under a hundred lines of script and markup

readings.reading: a few plain functions a reader follows at a glance
readings.in_practice: Named functions for place, win check, draw check and render, each short, sharing one array and one turn flag. At full strength they read aloud as the rules.

readings.reading: the fewest lines that still play
readings.in_practice: A compressed script that folds the win check into one expression over the eight triples. At full strength readability is traded for length: the whole game in a few dozen lines.
signals: under about forty lines of script

ds-basic.text: How people describe a basic game, and what each word tends to point at in the page.
behaviors: vanilla and bare-bones lean toward no framework and no styling
starter and first-cut lean toward a short build
toy version leans toward a round that is playable and nothing more

ds-game.text: How people refer to one playable round; the page is a single round, not a product or an engine.

rubber, from card games, names a best-of-three series; a deep cut for this page
